topics.title: Cartesian product and relation from A to B
notes: A × B = {(x, y) | x ∈ A and y ∈ B}: all ordered pairs with first element from A and second from B.
n(A × B) = n(A) · n(B). Example: A = {1, 2, 4}, B = {1, 3, 9} gives 3 × 3 = 9 pairs.
A × B and B × A are different sets in general (order of pairs matters).
A relation R from A to B is a subset of A × B. If (a, b) ∈ R, we write a R b (a is related to b).

topics.title: Domain and range of a relation
notes: Domain of R = set of all first elements a of the pairs (a, b) ∈ R.
Range of R = set of all second elements b of the pairs (a, b) ∈ R.
If R is a relation from A to B, then domain ⊆ A and range ⊆ B.

topics.title: Mapping and matrix representation of relations
notes: Mapping (arrow diagram): draw sets A and B as two ovals; for each (a, b) ∈ R draw an arrow from a to b.
Matrix representation: rows = elements of A, columns = elements of B. Entry 1 if (a, b) ∈ R, else 0.
Row 11 has all zeros because 11 is not less than any element of B.

topics.title: Relation on a set
notes: A relation on a set A is a subset of A × A.
If |A| = n, then |A × A| = n² and the number of relations on A is 2^(n²). For n = 3: 2^9 = 512.

topics.title: Reflexive and irreflexive relations
notes: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. Every element must have a self-pair.
Irreflexive: (a, a) ∉ R for every a ∈ A. No element may have a self-pair.
Neither: some (a, a) ∈ R and some (a, a) ∉ R. Example: a + b = 2 on {1, 2, 3, 4} gives R = {(1, 1)}, so it is neither.
a = b is reflexive. a < b and a > b are irreflexive.

topics.title: Symmetric and anti-symmetric relations
notes: Symmetric: if (a, b) ∈ R then (b, a) ∈ R. Check every pair; one missing reverse pair breaks symmetry.
Anti-symmetric: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R, then a = b. Equivalently, for a ≠ b, (a, b) ∈ R means (b, a) ∉ R.
A relation can be symmetric and anti-symmetric together (e.g. equality), or neither.
A relation is symmetric when its matrix is a symmetric matrix (A = Aᵀ).

topics.title: Transitive and compatibility relations
notes: Transitive: if (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R, then (a, c) ∈ R. Check all chains of two pairs.
Compatibility relation: reflexive and symmetric (transitivity is not needed).
Example: R = {(x, y) | x + y is an even integer} on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is a compatibility relation.

topics.title: Equivalence relation
notes: Equivalence relation = reflexive + symmetric + transitive.
Every equivalence relation is a compatibility relation, but not every compatibility relation is transitive.
Example: R = {(x, y) | x + y is divisible by 2} on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is reflexive (2x is even), symmetric and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.
Not an equivalence relation: x + y is odd on {1, ..., 6} is not reflexive, because 1 + 1 = 2 is even, so (1, 1) ∉ R.

topics.title: Partial order relation (POSET)
notes: Partial order = reflexive + anti-symmetric + transitive. The set with this relation is a POSET.
Example: x ≤ y on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is a POSET (reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive).
x > y is NOT a POSET because it is not reflexive (no pair (a, a)).

topics.title: Functions
notes: A function f: A → B is a relation from A to B such that every x ∈ A has exactly one image y ∈ B, written y = f(x).
A is the domain and B is the co-domain. Two different elements of A may have the same image.
Check: f(x) must be defined for every x in A and its value must lie in B. Example: f(x) = x + 2 on N is a function; f(x) = 1 − x on N is not (f(2) = −1 ∉ N).

topics.title: Composition of functions
notes: For f: X → Y and g: Y → Z, the composition g ∘ f: X → Z is defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Apply f first, then g.
Composition is generally NOT commutative: g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g in general.
Example: f(x) = x² and g(x) = x + 2 give (g ∘ f)(x) = x² + 2 and (f ∘ g)(x) = (x + 2)².
Method: substitute the inner function into the outer one. Example: f(x) = x + 3, g(x) = 3x − 4 gives (f ∘ g)(x) = 3x − 1 and (g ∘ f)(x) = 3x + 5.

None of (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) is in R, so R is irreflexive.

mcq.q: Is R = {(x, y) | x + y is divisible by 2} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} an equivalence relation?
mcq.explanation: x + x = 2x is always even, so R is reflexive. x + y = y + x makes it symmetric. Transitive because x + y even and y + z even means x and z have the same parity, so x + z is even.

mcq.explanation: POSET = reflexive + anti-symmetric + transitive.

mcq.q: Is R = {(x, y) | x > y} on A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} a POSET?
options: No, because it is not reflexive
No, because it is not transitive
mcq.explanation: x > x is false, so R is not reflexive and therefore not a POSET.

mcq.q: For a function f: A → B, every element of A has:
options: An image only if it is in B
mcq.explanation: Every x ∈ A has exactly one image f(x) ∈ B.

mcq.q: Is f(x) = 1 − x a function from N to N?
options: No, because f(1) = 0 and f(2) = −1 are not in N
No, because f(x) is not defined
mcq.explanation: 0 and −1 are not natural numbers, so f does not map N into N.

Define a reflexive relation and an irreflexive relation.
short.answer: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A. Irreflexive: (a, a) ∉ R for every a ∈ A.

short.q: Check whether R = {(1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is symmetric.
short.answer: No. (2, 3) ∈ R but (3, 2) ∉ R, so R is not symmetric.

short.q: Check whether R = {(1, 2), (2, 3)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is transitive.
short.answer: No. (1, 2) ∈ R and (2, 3) ∈ R, but (1, 3) ∉ R. So R is not transitive.

short.q: Check whether R = {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3)} on A = {1, 2, 3} is an equivalence relation.
short.answer: No. R is reflexive, but it is not symmetric: (2, 3) ∈ R while (3, 2) ∉ R. So R is not an equivalence relation.

short.q: Is R = {(x, y) | x ≤ y} on A = {1, 2, 3} a POSET? Give reasons.
short.answer: Yes. Reflexive: x ≤ x for all x. Anti-symmetric: x ≤ y and y ≤ x give x = y. Transitive: x ≤ y and y ≤ z give x ≤ z. So it is a POSET.

short.q: R = {(1, 2), (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 6)} is a relation from A = {1, 2, 3} to B = {2, 4, 6}. Is R a function?
short.answer: No. Element 1 of A has two images (2 and 4). A function must give each element of A exactly one image.
